"Al-sirr (the secret) is what is in the heart that one keeps hidden, and ﴿wa-akhfa﴾ (and more hidden) is that which He has not yet known [as it will occur]."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 20, verse 10:

It has been said: the verbal noun (al-masdar) is in construct with its agent (mudaf ila al-fa'il), meaning: "to remember You through it" (li-adhkuraka biha).

And it has been said: it is in construct with its object (mudaf ila al-madhkur), meaning: "so that you remember Me through it" (li-tadhkurunī biha). On this view, the lam is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil).

And it has been said: it is the temporal lam (al-lam al-waqtiyya), meaning: "establish the prayer at the time of My remembrance," like His saying: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾.

This meaning is intended by the verse, but interpreting it this way as its literal meaning is open to objection, because this temporal lam is ordinarily used with time-nouns and adverbial expressions of time.

The word dhikr is a verbal noun, unless a omitted time-noun is assumed, meaning: "at the time of My remembrance," and this is a possibility.

The most apparent view is that it is the lam of causation, meaning: "establish the prayer for the sake of My remembrance." It follows from this that establishing it occurs at the time of His remembrance, and when the servant remembers his Lord, God's remembrance of him precedes his remembrance of Him, for when He remembered him, He inspired him to remember Him. So the three meanings are all true.

(A Subtle Point)

Abu Ali al-Daqqaq said: The murid (the seeker who is striving) is one who bears the burden, and the murad (the one who is sought/chosen) is one who is carried. Musa ﷺ was a murid when he said: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾.

Our Prophet ﷺ was a murad, when it was said to him: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1].

Al-Junayd was asked about the murid and the murad.

He said: The murid—his governance is entrusted to knowledge.

And the murad—his care is entrusted to the Truth, because the murid walks, and the murad flies.

So when does the walker reach the flier?

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 20, verses 38–39:

Al-Suhayli said: Among the benefits of this question is that we ask: why did the first verse come with (ʿalā, "upon") while the second came with the letter bāʾ (bi, "with")?

The answer: we must inquire about the meaning for which God, exalted is He, said ﴿and that you might be brought up under My eye﴾ with the particle (ʿalā), and said ﴿they sail under Our eyes﴾ and ﴿construct the ark under Our eyes﴾ with the particle bāʾ. What is the difference?

It is said: the difference is that the first verse came to manifest a matter that had been hidden and to reveal what had been concealed. Children at that time were nourished and reared in secret, so when God willed that Moses, peace be upon him, be made and nourished and raised in a state of safety and openness, not under fear and concealment, the particle (ʿalā) entered the wording to indicate this meaning, because it conveys elevation, and elevation is manifestness and disclosure. It is as if He, glorified and exalted, were saying: "and that you be made upon safety, not under fear." The mention of the eye is because it includes the meaning of care and protection.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they sail under Our eyes﴾ and ﴿construct the ark under Our eyes﴾, He intends only with care from Us and protection, and does not intend the disclosure of anything or its manifestation after concealment. Therefore there was no need in the wording for the meaning of (ʿalā), unlike what preceded. This is his statement. He, may God have mercy on him, did not address the reason for the singular in the former place and the plural here, and it is among the subtlest meanings of the verse. The difference between them becomes apparent from the distinction bestowed upon Moses in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and I have chosen you for Myself﴾. This distinction required the further distinction in His saying ﴿and that you might be brought up under My eye﴾, for this addition is an addition of particularization.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they sail under Our eyes﴾ and ﴿construct the ark under Our eyes﴾, there is not in it the particularization found in Moses being made under the eye of God, glorified and exalted, and His choosing him for Himself. What He attributes to Himself with the plural pronoun may intend His angels, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so when We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾ and His saying ﴿We relate to you﴾ and their like. So reflect on it.

He said: As for the word "nafs" (self), in its original usage it is an expression of the reality of existence without any additional meaning. Derivatives of its root have also been used, such as nafāsah (preciousness) and nafīs (precious thing), so it is suitable to express God, glorified and exalted, by it, unlike the figurative terms mentioned earlier. As for "dhāt" (essence), most people, especially the theologians (mutakallimūn), have been drawn to the view that it means the same as nafs and reality. They say the essence of the Creator is His self, and they express by it His existence and reality, and they argue for this usage by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "In the story of Abraham there were three lies, all of them concerning the essence of God (fī dhāt Allāh)."

Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

And the saying of Khubayb: "and that was for the sake of the essence of the God (dhāt al-ilāh)." He said: This word, when one surveys its use in the language and the Law, is not as they claim. If it were so, it would be permissible to say "near the essence of God" or "beware the essence of God," as God, exalted is He, said ﴿and God warns you of Himself (nafsahu)﴾. That is not heard, and it is not said except with the preposition bi (in/with) or fī (in), and fī is for containment, a meaning impossible for the self of the Creator, exalted is He. When you say "I struggled in God, exalted is He" or "I loved you in God, exalted is He," it is impossible that this expression be literal, because of what this particle indicates of the meaning of containment. It is rather with an elided genitive, i.e., "for the pleasure of God and His obedience," so the particle remains in its proper sense, as if you said: "this is beloved in the deeds in which is the pleasure of God and His obedience." As for leaving the expression on its apparent sense, that is impossible. Once this is established, his saying "in the essence of God" or "in the essence of the God" intends "in the religion and the Law which is the essence of the God," so dhāt is a qualifier of the religion. Likewise, in its original usage it is an adjective of a feminine noun; do you not see that it has the feminine tā' marker? When this is the case, it has become an expression of what is honoured by its relation to God, exalted is He, not of His self, glorified is He. This is what is understood from the speech of the Arabs. Do you not see the saying of al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani:

They exalted them, the essence of God, and their religion

Thus the error of one who makes this word an expression of the very self of what it is attributed to has become evident. This is among his playful remarks, in which he did as he pleased.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 20, verse 40:

His saying, ﴿And We tested you with a [severe] testing﴾, means: We afflicted you, tested you, and turned you through the states that Allah, glorified is He, related to us, from the time of his birth until the time He spoke to him and sent down His Book upon him.

[Section: The Station of the Time (waqt)]

The author of al-Manazil said:

The chapter on the Time (al-waqt). Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Then you came [at a set time], O Moses﴾.

Time (al-waqt) is a name for the vessel of existence (zarf al-kawn).

In this chapter it is a name for three meanings, on three levels.

The first meaning: a moment of true ecstasy (wajd), to the intimacy of the light of a grace drawn out by the clarity of hope, or to a protection drawn out by the truthfulness of fear, or to the blazing of longing drawn out by the kindling of love.

The manner in which he cites the verse as evidence: Allah, glorified is He, decreed the coming of Moses at the moment when the time was most in need of it. For the Arabs say: "So-and-so came according to a measure (ʿalā qadar)," when the time of need for him has come.

Jarir said:

؎He attained the caliphate when it was at its appointed time, / just as Moses came to his Lord at an appointed time

And Mujahid said: "at an appointment" (ʿalā mawʿid). But this is open to scrutiny, because no appointment for the coming had preceded between Allah, glorified is He, and Moses, so that it could be said that he came at that appointment.

Rather, the meaning is: you came at the appointment which We promised to fulfil, and the measure which We decreed to occur at its time. This is like His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down upon their faces in prostration, and say: "Glory be to our Lord; indeed the promise of our Lord has been fulfilled"﴾ [al-Isra: 107-108], because Allah, glorified and exalted is He, had promised to send a Prophet at the end of time who would fill the earth with light and guidance. So when they heard the Qur'an, they knew that Allah had fulfilled that promise which He had made.

His citing of this verse indicates his station in knowledge, because when a thing occurs in its time, which is the most fitting of times for its occurrence, it is better, more beneficial and more fruitful, just as when rain falls at the time when people are most in need of it, and just as when relief comes at the time that befits it.

Whoever reflects on the decrees of the Lord, exalted is He, and their operation among creation, knows that they occur at the most fitting of times for them.

So Allah, glorified is He, sent Moses when people were most in need of his mission; and He sent Jesus likewise; and He sent Muhammad (ﷺ), upon him and upon them all, when the people of the earth were most in need of his sending. Likewise, the time of the servate with Allah is one in which He builds him up with the most beneficial of things for him, at the moment when he most needs its building up.

His saying, "Time: the vessel of existence" — time is an expression, according to the theologians (al-mutakallimun), for the proximity of one occurrence to another, so it is a relation between two occurrences.

So his saying "the vessel of existence" means the receptacle of creation (wiʿa' al-takwin).

It is the temporal receptacle in which creation takes place, just as the vessel of place is the spatial receptacle in which a body is located.

However, time in the terminology of the people (i.e., the Sufis) is more specific than that.

Abu ʿAli al-Daqqaq said: "Time is what you are in. If you are in this world, your time is this world; if you are in the Hereafter, your time is the Hereafter. If you are in joy, your time is joy; if you are in sorrow, your time is sorrow."

He means: time is the state that predominates over a person.

It may also mean: time is what lies between the two periods, the past and the future. This is the terminology of most of the group. For this reason they say: "The Sufi and the poor man are the son of their time (ibn waqtihi)."

They mean: his aspiration does not exceed the duty of building up his time with what is most fitting and most beneficial for him. He is occupied with what he is required to do in the present moment. He does not concern himself with the past or future of his time, but with the time in which he is. Occupation with past and future time loses the present time, and whenever a time arrives he is distracted from it by both extremes, so all his times become lost.

Al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I accompanied the Sufis, and I benefited from them only two words. I heard them say: 'Time is a sword: if you do not cut it, it will cut you. And the self: if you do not occupy it with the truth, it will occupy you with falsehood.'"

I say: How excellent are these two words, how beneficial and comprehensive they are, and how much they indicate the loftiness of aspiration and vigilance of their speaker.

The praise of al-Shafiʿi for the group is sufficient for this, given the measure of their words.

They may also mean by time something more specific than all of this: that which befalls them in the Truth's disposal of them, not what they choose for themselves. They say: "So-and-so is under the judgment of time," meaning he submits to what comes from Allah without choice.

This is good in one state, forbidden in another, and blameworthy for its possessor in another. It is good in every place where Allah has no command or prohibition upon the servant, but rather in the place of the operation of the universal decree (al-hukm al-kawni), which is not connected to any command or prohibition, such as poverty, sickness, estrangement, hunger, pain, heat and cold, and the like.

It is forbidden in the state in which command, prohibition and the performance of the rights of the Law apply to him. For neglecting these, submitting, and drifting with the decree is a complete withdrawal from religion. It is blameworthy for its possessor in a state which calls for standing in supererogatory acts and various kinds of righteousness and obedience.

When Allah wills good for a servant, He helps him through time, and makes his time a helper for him. When He wills evil for him, He makes his time a burden upon him, and his time troubles him. So whenever he intends to prepare for the journey, time does not assist him; and in the first case, whenever his soul desires to sit idle, time raises him up and assists him.

Some of them divided the Sufis into four categories: the people of antecedence (al-sawabiq), the people of consequences (al-ʿawaqib), the people of time (al-waqt), and the people of truth (al-haqq). He said:

As for the people of antecedence: their hearts are always with what was previously decreed for them by Allah, knowing that the eternal judgment does not change by the servant's acquisition.

They say: "Whom antecedence has distanced, means will not bring near." So their thought is always on this. Yet they strive in performing the commands, avoiding the prohibitions, and drawing near to Allah by various kinds of acts of nearness, not trusting in them nor relying upon them. Their speaker says:

؎From where shall I please You, unless You grant me success? / Far, far! Success does not come from me.

؎If I have no antecedence in what is decreed, / then the deeds I have sent forth will not benefit me.

As for the people of consequences: they reflect on how their affairs will end, for matters are judged by their endings, deeds by their conclusions, and the outcome is hidden.

As it has been said:

؎Let not the clarity of times deceive you, / for beneath it are hidden calamities.

How many a spring whose trees bloomed, whose flowers opened, and whose fruits became good, yet soon a heavenly calamity struck it, and it became as Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿until, when the earth has taken its adornment and become beautified, and its people think they have power over it﴾ [Yunus: 24] — up to His saying — ﴿who reflect﴾ [Yunus: 24].

؎How many an aspirant has been thrown by the steed of his resolve, / and fallen prostrate upon his hands and his mouth.

It was said to one of them, when he was seen acting contrary to what he was known for: "What has befallen you?" He said: "A veil has fallen," and he recited:

؎You thought well of the days when they were good, / and did not fear the evil that fate might bring.

؎The nights were at peace with you, so you were deceived by them, / yet in the clarity of the nights, turbidity arises.

The wonder is not at one who perished, how he perished; rather the wonder is at one who was saved, how he was saved?

؎You marvel at my sickness, / my health is the marvel.

Those who turn back upon their heels are many times more than those who break through the steep path:

؎Take one from a thousand, / and discard all the rest after him.

As for the people of time: they do not occupy themselves with antecedence or consequences, but with observing the time and what its rulings require of them. They say: "The knower is the son of his time: he has neither past nor future."

Some of them saw al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, in a dream. He said to him: "Advise me." He said: "Be the son of your time."

As for the people of truth: they are with the owner of time and the era, its master and manager, absorbed in witnessing Him through beholding the times. They have no leisure to observe a time or an era. As it has been said:

؎I do not know whether my night has lengthened or not; / how can one who is tormented know of that?

؎Had I been free to measure the lengthening of my night, / and to watch the stars, I would have been idle.

؎Indeed for lovers, from the brevity of the night / and from its length, there is an occupation through love.

Al-Junayd said: "I entered upon al-Sari one day, and said to him: 'How did you wake up?' Then he composed:

؎In the day nor in the night is there relief for me, / so I care not whether the night has lengthened or shortened."

Then he said: "With your Lord there is neither night nor day."

He points out that he is not longing for times, but rather is with the One who decreed night and day.

Istina'a (al-istina', "making someone a protégé"), in its root sense, means "making a favour" (ṣanī'a), which is a kindness you bestow on another. The poet said:

"When you bestow a favour, do so seeking the face of Him who grants all favours, [and] you will be preserved."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "I have chosen you for My revelation and My message." al-Kalbi said: "I have chosen you with the message for Myself, so that you love Me and carry out My command."

It is also said: "I have chosen you, by bestowing kindness upon you, to establish My proof, so that you may speak to My servants on My behalf."

Abu Ishaq said: "I have chosen you by bestowing kindness upon you, to establish My proof, and I have made you between Me and My creation, until in address and conveying [My message] on My behalf you occupy the station that I would occupy were I to address them myself."

It is also said: his condition is likened to that of one whom a king sees as possessing comprehensive qualities and distinctive traits fit for his honour and nearness. No one is closer to him in rank, nor more intimate in station, so he makes him his protégé with honour and special favour, and singles him out for himself, to the point that he hears through him, sees through him, and is made aware of his secret.

God Most High said to His interlocutor Musa and his brother Harun: ﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh; indeed he has transgressed.﴾ (43) ﴿And speak to him with gentle speech; perhaps he will be reminded or fear.﴾ (44)

So God commanded them to speak gently to the greatest of His enemies, the most severe of them in disbelief and the most insolent toward Him, lest harsh speech to him, even though he deserved it, become a means of repelling him and of his not being patient in the establishment of the proof. Thus He forbade them what was permissible, lest there result from it what is more hateful to Him, Exalted is He.

**Benefit: The placing of "hearing" before "seeing" has two reasons.**

The first is that the context calls for it, such that mentioning these two attributes together carries a threat and a warning, as is the custom of the Qur'an: it threatens and cautions its addressees by mentioning attributes of His that call for vigilance and uprightness. Such as His saying: ﴿And know that if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾, and His saying: ﴿Whoever should desire the reward of this world — with Allah is the reward of this world and the Hereafter. And ever is Allah Hearing and Seeing﴾. The Noble Qur'an is full of this. On this basis, there is included within it: "I hear what they answer you with, and what they oppose My messages with, and I see what they do." There is no doubt that those addressed by the message are of two kinds with regard to response and obedience:

The first received it with the words "You have spoken the truth," and then acted in accordance with its requirement.

The second received it with denial and then acted contrary to it. So the rank of what is heard from them comes before the rank of what is seen, and what relates to hearing is placed before what relates to seeing.

Reflect on this meaning in the words of Allah, Exalted, to Moses: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾. He hears what they answer him with, and sees what they do.

This does not apply to all passages; rather, it is specific to those cases whose circumstances are of this kind.

The second reason is that denying the false illusions regarding the hearing of speech, despite the extreme distance between the hearer and the heard, is more severe than denying their seeing it despite that distance.

In the Two Sahihs, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said:

"Three men gathered at the House: two Thaqafis and a Qurashi, or two Qurashis and a Thaqafi. One of them said: 'Do you think Allah hears what we say?' The second said: 'He hears if we speak aloud, and does not hear if we conceal it.' The third said: 'If He hears when we speak aloud, then He hears when we conceal it.'"

Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi.

They did not say, "Do you think Allah sees us?" So the mention of hearing was more important, and the need to know it was more pressing.

A third reason is that the movement of the tongue in speech is the greatest of the movements of the limbs and the most powerful in its effect on good and evil, righteousness and corruption. Indeed, most of the actions that come to exist in the world arise only after the movement of the tongue. Therefore, mentioning the attribute related to it was more important and more fitting.

From this it is known that it is placed before "the All-Knowing" wherever it occurs.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 20, verse 47:

If it is said: What is the wisdom in the Prophet ﷺ greeting, in his letter to Heraclius, "peace upon those who follow the guidance" with an indefinite noun, while Moses greeted [Pharaoh] with a definite noun?

The answer to this is that the Prophet's ﷺ greeting is an initiatory greeting (taslim ibtida'i), and for this reason the letter opened with it, where he said: "From Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Heraclius, the great one of the Romans: Peace upon those who follow the guidance." So in its indefiniteness there is the same wisdom as in the indefiniteness of "salam" (peace), and its explanation has already been given. As for the words of Moses, "and peace upon those who follow the guidance," this is not a greeting of salutation, for Pharaoh did not initiate it; rather it is a pure statement of fact. Indeed, those who follow the guidance have absolute peace, unlike those who oppose it. For he said to him: ﴿So send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them. We have come to you with a sign from your Lord. And peace will be upon those who follow the guidance. Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment will be upon him who denies and turns away.﴾ Do you not see that this is not a greeting at the beginning of speech nor at its end? It occurs only in the middle between two statements, as a pure report of the descent and settling of safety upon those who follow the guidance. In it there is an invitation to Pharaoh and an encouragement with what souls are created to love and prefer, namely safety, and that if he follows the guidance brought to him, he is among the people of peace. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Consider the excellent arrangement of these sentences and the ordering of this address, and the gentleness of this speech, whose beauty and sweetness captivate hearts despite its majesty and grandeur: how he began the address with the words ﴿Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord﴾. Implicit in this is: we have not come to dispute your kingdom, nor to make you a partner in it; rather we are two servants, commanded and sent from your Lord to you.

In attributing the name "Lord" (al-Rabb) to him here, and not attributing it to both of them, there is an invitation to his hearing, obedience and acceptance, just as a messenger says to a man from his master: "I am the messenger of your master (mawlak) to you and your teacher (ustadhak)," even though he is the teacher of both of them together; but by attributing it to him he alerts him to listen and obey. Al-Kalbi and al-Suddi said: "He gave the man the woman, the camel the she-camel, and the male the female of its kind."

This view was chosen by Ibn Qutaybah and al-Farraʾ.

Al-Farraʾ said: "He gave the male among people a woman like him, the sheep a sheep, and the bull a cow, then inspired the male how to approach her."

Abu Ishaq said: "This interpretation is permissible, because we see the male among animals approach the female, and we have not seen a male who had approached a female before him; so God inspired him with that and guided him to it."

He said: "The first view encompasses this meaning, because when He guides it to its benefit, this falls within the benefit."

This pigeon is among the most remarkable of animals in its guidance, to the extent that al-Shafi'i said: "The most intelligent of birds is the pigeon."

Carrier pigeons, which carry messages and letters, are sometimes valued more highly than a slave or a servant, because the purpose they achieve cannot be achieved by a slave or any other animal. It goes off and returns to its place from a distance of a thousand farsakhs or less. Through it, the news, aims and intentions on which the vital affairs of kingdoms and states depend are conveyed. Those in charge of its affairs take great care over its lineages. They separate its males from its females at the time of mating, and move males away from females and females away from males to others. They fear for them the corruption of their lineages and their being impregnated by others. They verify the soundness of their paths and their origins. They do not feel safe that a female might be corrupted by a male from among the common pigeons, so that she would suffer hybridity. Yet those in charge of the affairs of humans do not guard the wombs of their women as they guard the wombs of their pigeons, nor take as many precautions for them. Those who manage the pigeons have rules and methods which they observe with the utmost care, so that when they see a pigeon that has fallen, they do not fail to know its stock, its lineage, and its place of origin. They honour the one who has experience and knowledge, and they willingly give him a generous reward. For carrying letters and messages they choose the males, saying: "He is more attached to his home because of his female, he is stronger in constitution and body, and better at finding his way." A group among them chooses the females for this, saying: "When the male travels and has been away for a long time, he yearns for the females and his soul longs for them. Perhaps he sees a female on his route or on his way back, and cannot restrain himself from her, so he abandons the journey and turns to satisfy his desire from her." His guidance depends on the degree of training and habituation. The pigeon is characterised by good fortune (al-yumn), and it is sociable with people. It loves people and they love it. It becomes attached to a place and remains faithful to its master's trust even if he treats it badly. It returns to him from great distances, and perhaps it is kept away and leaves its homeland for ten years, yet it remains steadfast in its loyalty until it finds an opportunity and the ability, and then it returns to him.

When the pigeon wishes to mate, it treats the female with the utmost gentleness. It begins by spreading its tail and lowering its wing, then draws near to the female, coos to her, mounts her, and puffs up and raises its chest. Then a kind of ecstasy overtakes it. The female, in this, lowers her wing and shoulder to the ground. When the male has satisfied his need from her, the female rises beneath him. This does not occur in any other animal. When the male knows that he has deposited in the female's womb that which will become a child, he and the female set about gathering reeds, grass and small twigs. From these they build a nest, weaving them tightly together in the shape that matches the size of a dove's body, and they make its edges raised and elevated so that the eggs will not roll out of it, and so that it will be a shelter for the one who incubates them. Then they return repeatedly to that place, and they take turns in the nest, warming and perfuming it, removing its original nature and creating in it a new nature derived and extracted from the natures and scents of their own bodies. This is so that, when the egg is laid, it falls in a place most resembling the wombs of pigeons, with a degree of heat, cold, softness and firmness. Then when the pains of labour seize her, she hastens to that place and lays the egg in it. If a violent thunderclap frightens her, she casts the egg away from the place she had prepared, like a woman who miscarries from fear. When she lays the eggs in that place, the two of them keep taking turns at incubating until the period of incubation reaches its end and its days are complete. The chick then breaks out of the shell, and they help it to emerge. First they blow air into its throat so that its crop (hawsala) widens, knowing that the crop is too narrow for food, so the crop widens after its joining, and opens up after being closed. Then they know that although the crop has widened somewhat, at first it cannot bear food, so they feed it with their saliva mixed with food, which contains the powers of taste. Then they know that the nature of the crop is too weak to sustain continuous feeding, and that it needs support and strengthening so that it may have some firmness. So they pick up soft, tender grains from the fields and feed them to the chick. Afterwards they feed it harder and stronger grain, and they continue to feed it grain and water gradually, according to the chick's strength, and it asks them for this. When they know that it is able to pick up grain for itself, they somewhat withhold food from it, so that it has to search for food and become accustomed to doing so. When they know that its lungs have grown strong and developed, and that if they wean it completely it will be strong enough to pick up grain and provide for itself, they strike it when it asks them for food and refuse it. Then that wondrous tenderness departs from them, and they forget that compassion which had been firmly established in them, once they know that it is able to stand on its own and earn its living. Then they begin the work afresh in this same order.

The pigeon resembles people in most of its natures and ways. Among its females is one who will accept only her husband. Among them is another who will not turn away from any hand that touches her. Another cannot be obtained except after a persistent pursuit. Another mounts at the very first encounter and the first solicitation. Another is known for a particular male, but when her husband is absent she allows another male to mount her, and does not refuse whoever mounts her. Another allows someone who will satisfy her in place of her husband, while he watches and observes them, and she does not care about his presence. Another shakes out the male and calls him to herself. There is a female that mounts another female and rubs against her, and a male that mounts a male and forces him. Every condition found among men and women is found among the pigeons. Among them is one that does not lay eggs, and if she does lay them she spoils the egg, like a woman who does not want children so that they will not distract her from her affairs. Among the female pigeons is one who, if any male approaches her, whatever kind he is, flees quickly and will not yield to anyone but her husband, just like a free woman. Among them is one that takes a female and enjoys her, then moves on from her to another. Likewise, a female may go from her husband to another male, and move on from him, even if they are all in the same dovecote. Among them are males who compete over a female, two or more, and she mixes with all of them until one of them overcomes his companion and subdues him, and then she inclines to him and turns away from the defeated one.

In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) saw a dove following a dove, and said: "A devil follows its devil."

Among them is one that feeds only its own young, and among them is one that has great compassion and feeds its young and others.

Among the marvels of its guidance is that when it carries messages, it takes distant routes away from villages and places where people live, so that no one who wishes to stop it encounters it. It does not drink from the waters of people, but drinks from waters that people do not frequent. Another part of its guidance is that when it sees people in the air, it recognises which kind it is aiming for and which kind is its enemy, so it changes its course to avoid them. Another aspect of its guidance is that at the beginning of its flight it is careless, and passes between the eagle and the vulture, between the vulture and the falcon, and between the crow and the hawk, recognising which of them is targeting it and which is not. If it sees the shaheen (a kind of falcon), it is as though it sees deadly poison, and it is seized with confusion, just as a sheep is when it sees a wolf, or a donkey when it sees a lion.

Another part of the guidance of the pigeon is that the male and the female share the care of the young. Incubation, rearing and protection fall to the female, while bringing food and feeding fall to the male, for the father is the head of the household and its provider, and the mother is the one who conceives, gives birth and nurses.

Among the wonders of its behaviour is what al-Jahiz mentioned: a man had a pair of clipped-winged pigeons and a pair of flying pigeons, and the flying pair had two chicks. He said: "I opened for them a window at the top of the room for entering and leaving, and they fed their chicks." He said: "Then the sultan suddenly imprisoned me, and I was greatly troubled about the clipped pair, and I did not doubt that they would die, since they could not get out through the window and had nothing to eat or drink." He said: "When I was released, I had no concern but for them. I opened the room and found the chicks had grown, and found the clipped pair in the best condition. I was amazed. Shortly after, the flying male came, and the clipped male drew close to their mouths, asking to be fed as a chick asks, and they fed them. Look at this guidance: when the clipped pair saw the tenderness of the chicks towards their parents, and how they asked to be fed when hunger and thirst overcame them, they acted as the two chicks had acted. The compassion of the flying pair seized them, and they fed them just as they fed their own chicks."

A similar account is what al-Jahiz and others mentioned. Al-Jahiz said: "It is a well-known matter among us in Basra that when the great plague (al-ta'un al-jarif) struck, it affected a household, and the people of that quarter did not doubt that none of them remained. So they went to the door of the house and sealed it. But a small child who was still nursing had remained, and they had not noticed him. Some time later, some of the heirs of that family moved into it. They opened the door, and when they reached the courtyard of the house, they found a child playing with the puppies of a bitch that had belonged to the household. This startled them. Then the bitch itself came, and when the child saw her he crawled towards her, and she let him reach her teats, and he suckled. For when the child's hunger had grown intense, and he saw the puppies suckling from the bitch's teats, he crawled towards her, and she was moved to him. When she first let him suckle, she continued to do so, and he continued to seek it."

This is not to be thought unlikely, and there is something even more remarkable than it. For He who guided the newborn to suck its thumb at the moment of birth, then guided it to take hold of the nipple, without any prior habit, is as though he had been told: "This is the storehouse of your food and drink, which you have always known." And in His guidance of animals to what suits them there is something even more wonderful than that.

Among this is that a young cockerel, when it finds grain, does not eat it until it has scattered it. But when it becomes old and decrepit, it eats it without scattering it, as al-Mada'ini related:

"Iyas ibn Mu'awiya passed by a cockerel pecking at grain without scattering it. He said: 'It must be old. The young cockerel scatters the grain so that the hens gather around it and get some of it. But the old one has lost its desire, and has no concern except for itself.' Iyas said: 'The cockerel takes a grain and shows it to the hen until it drops it from its beak, whereas the old one swallows it and does not drop it for the hen.'"

Ibn al-A'rabi related: "I ate an egg of a makka (a kind of bird). The makka began to cry out and fly over my head, approaching me, until when I opened my mouth and was about to eat it, it dropped a thorn, which caught in my throat, and I died."

Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani recited in this regard the verse of al-Asadi:

*If you have seen me poor and destitute, / then often the makka has killed a serpent.*

The guidance of animals to the interests of their livelihood is like the sea: speak of it and there is no blame.

Then that wondrous tenderness departs from them, and they forget that compassion which had been firmly established in them, once they know that it is able to stand on its own and earn its living. Then they begin the work afresh in this same order.

The pigeon resembles people in most of its natures and ways. Among its females is one who will accept only her husband. Among them is another who will not turn away from any hand that touches her. Another cannot be obtained except after a persistent pursuit. Another mounts at the very first encounter and the first solicitation. Another is known for a particular male, but when her husband is absent she allows another male to mount her, and does not refuse whoever mounts her. Another allows someone who will satisfy her in place of her husband, while he watches and observes them, and she does not care about his presence. Another shakes out the male and calls him to herself. There is a female that mounts another female and rubs against her, and a male that mounts a male and forces him. Every condition found among men and women is found among the pigeons. Among them is one that does not lay eggs, and if she does lay them she spoils the egg, like a woman who does not want children so that they will not distract her from her affairs. Among the female pigeons is one who, if any male approaches her, whatever kind he is, flees quickly and will not yield to anyone but her husband, just like a free woman. Among them is one that takes a female and enjoys her, then moves on from her to another. Likewise, a female may go from her husband to another male, and move on from him, even if they are all in the same dovecote. Among them are males who compete over a female, two or more, and she mixes with all of them until one of them overcomes his companion and subdues him, and then she inclines to him and turns away from the defeated one.

In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) saw a dove following a dove, and said: "A devil follows its devil."

Among them is one that feeds only its own young, and among them is one that has great compassion and feeds its young and others.

Among the marvels of its guidance is that when it carries messages, it takes distant routes away from villages and places where people live, so that no one who wishes to stop it encounters it. It does not drink from the waters of people, but drinks from waters that people do not frequent. Another part of its guidance is that when it sees people in the air, it recognises which kind it is aiming for and which kind is its enemy, so it changes its course to avoid them. Another aspect of its guidance is that at the beginning of its flight it is careless, and passes between the eagle and the vulture, between the vulture and the falcon, and between the crow and the hawk, recognising which of them is targeting it and which is not. If it sees the shaheen (a kind of falcon), it is as though it sees deadly poison, and it is seized with confusion, just as a sheep is when it sees a wolf, or a donkey when it sees a lion.

Another part of the guidance of the pigeon is that the male and the female share the care of the young. Incubation, rearing and protection fall to the female, while bringing food and feeding fall to the male, for the father is the head of the household and its provider, and the mother is the one who conceives, gives birth and nurses.

Among the wonders of its behaviour is what al-Jahiz mentioned: a man had a pair of clipped-winged pigeons and a pair of flying pigeons, and the flying pair had two chicks. He said: "I opened for them a window at the top of the room for entering and leaving, and they fed their chicks." He said: "Then the sultan suddenly imprisoned me, and I was greatly troubled about the clipped pair, and I did not doubt that they would die, since they could not get out through the window and had nothing to eat or drink." He said: "When I was released, I had no concern but for them. I opened the room and found the chicks had grown, and found the clipped pair in the best condition. I was amazed. Shortly after, the flying male came, and the clipped male drew close to their mouths, asking to be fed as a chick asks, and they fed them. Look at this guidance: when the clipped pair saw the tenderness of the chicks towards their parents, and how they asked to be fed when hunger and thirst overcame them, they acted as the two chicks had acted. The compassion of the flying pair seized them, and they fed them just as they fed their own chicks."

A similar account is what al-Jahiz and others mentioned. Al-Jahiz said: "It is a well-known matter among us in Basra that when the great plague (al-ta'un al-jarif) struck, it affected a household, and the people of that quarter did not doubt that none of them remained. So they went to the door of the house and sealed it. But a small child who was still nursing had remained, and they had not noticed him. Some time later, some of the heirs of that family moved into it. They opened the door, and when they reached the courtyard of the house, they found a child playing with the puppies of a bitch that had belonged to the household. This startled them. Then the bitch itself came, and when the child saw her he crawled towards her, and she let him reach her teats, and he suckled. For when the child's hunger had grown intense, and he saw the puppies suckling from the bitch's teats, he crawled towards her, and she was moved to him. When she first let him suckle, she continued to do so, and he continued to seek it."

This is not to be thought unlikely, and there is something even more remarkable than it. For He who guided the newborn to suck its thumb at the moment of birth, then guided it to take hold of the nipple, without any prior habit, is as though he had been told: "This is the storehouse of your food and drink, which you have always known." And in His guidance of animals to what suits them there is something even more wonderful than that.

Among this is that a young cockerel, when it finds grain, does not eat it until it has scattered it. But when it becomes old and decrepit, it eats it without scattering it, as al-Mada'ini related:

"Iyas ibn Mu'awiya passed by a cockerel pecking at grain without scattering it. He said: 'It must be old. The young cockerel scatters the grain so that the hens gather around it and get some of it. But the old one has lost its desire, and has no concern except for itself.' Iyas said: 'The cockerel takes a grain and shows it to the hen until it drops it from its beak, whereas the old one swallows it and does not drop it for the hen.'"

Ibn al-A'rabi related: "I ate an egg of a makka (a kind of bird). The makka began to cry out and fly over my head, approaching me, until when I opened my mouth and was about to eat it, it dropped a thorn, which caught in my throat, and I died."

Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani recited in this regard the verse of al-Asadi:

*If you have seen me poor and destitute, / then often the makka has killed a serpent.*

The guidance of animals to the interests of their livelihood is like the sea: speak of it and there is no blame.

(Admonition)

Do not neglect the care of the magicians. They came to wage war against Moses and against his messengers, and the treaty of peace had been detailed and the crowns of contentment had been placed. The drink of union had been passed around, so they stretched out their hands toward what they had pressed from the wine of passion, and behold, it had turned into vinegar. So they distilled upon it and became intoxicated with the drink of love. When love became violent with them, they were crucified on the trunks of palm trees. How wondrous are resolves that nothing can turn back: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on alternate sides﴾.

They prostrated to Him in a single prostration, and they did not raise their heads until they saw their dwellings in Paradise. Ecstasy overcame them and longing took hold of them, so they said: ﴿Decree whatever you will decree; you can only decree concerning this worldly life.﴾

Ah, the Ṣabā breeze passes over the one who dwells in al-Ghaḍā, and my heart is split open by its blowing.

Near is the time since they were with the Beloved, but the desire of every soul is wherever its beloved dwells.

The camels of their grandfather traversed the desert by night, yet they did not feel the weariness of travel, for the road to the Beloved is not long.

Far is it for the lazy one or the one who is bored, but for the yearning lover, it is near.

(Benefit)

Pleasure follows love: it grows with its strength and weakens with its weakness. Therefore, whenever the desire for the Beloved and longing for Him is stronger, the pleasure of reaching Him is more complete. Love and longing follow knowledge of Him and awareness of Him, so whenever knowledge of Him is more complete, His love is more perfect. When the perfection of bliss in the Hereafter and the perfection of pleasure return to knowledge and love, then whoever believes in Allah, His names, His attributes, and His religion more deeply will love Him more, and his pleasure in reaching Him through His nearness, gazing upon His Face, and hearing His speech will be more complete. Every pleasure, bliss, joy, and delight in comparison with that is like a drop in an ocean. So how could one who has intellect prefer a weak, brief pleasure mixed with pains over a great pleasure that lasts for eternity without end? The servant's perfection is according to these two powers, knowledge and love, and the best knowledge is knowledge of Allah, the highest love is love for Him, and the perfection of pleasure is according to these two. And Allah is the One sought for help.

(A Great Benefit)

One finds hardship only in abandoning habits and customs when one abandons them for other than Allah. As for one who abandons them sincerely and devotedly for Allah from his heart, he finds no hardship in abandoning them except at the very first moment, to test whether he is truthful or lying in abandoning them. If he is patient through that hardship for a little while, it turns into pleasure.

Ibn Sīrīn said: "I heard Shurayḥ swear by Allah that no servant ever abandoned anything for Allah and then found its loss."

Their saying, "Whoever abandons something for Allah, Allah will compensate him with something better than it," is true, and the compensation takes various forms. The most sublime of what one is compensated with is intimacy with Allah, love for Him, tranquility of the heart in Him, its strength, its vigor, its joy, and its contentment with its Lord, exalted is He.

The most foolish of people is the one who goes astray at the end of his journey when he is near the destination.

[Section: Preferring What Is Most Beneficial]

Each of the voluntary acts and voluntary abstentions is preferred by a living being only because of the benefit it brings, through which it takes pleasure, or because of the removal of a pain, by whose removal it attains healing. For this reason it is said: "He healed his chest" and "He healed his heart." And someone said:

"They are the cure for my ailment, if only I could obtain them, but the cure for the disease is not freely available from them."

This is a goal that the intelligent person prefers, indeed even the grazing animal prefers it. However, most people err in it with a terrible error: they aim to obtain pleasure through something that leads to the greatest pain, so they cause themselves pain while thinking they are obtaining its pleasure, and they heal their hearts through something that brings about the utmost sickness. This is the condition of one who restricts his vision to the immediate and does not consider the consequences, especially the intellect that looks at consequences. The most intelligent of people is the one who prefers his pleasure and ease in the lasting Hereafter over the fleeting, passing worldly life. The most foolish of creatures is the one who sells the eternal bliss, the good of everlasting life, and the supreme pleasure in which there is no disturbance or deficiency in any way, for a fleeting pleasure mixed with pains and fears, which is quick to vanish and soon to end.

Some scholars said: "I reflected on what the intelligent people strive for, and I saw that all of them strive for one goal, though their methods of attaining it differ. I saw that all of them strive to repel distress and grief from themselves. This one does it through eating and drinking, this one through trade and earning, this one through marriage, this one through listening to music and stirring voices, and this one through amusement and play. So I said: 'This is the goal sought by the intelligent, but all these paths do not lead to it; rather, most of them lead only to its opposite. I have found among all these paths no path that leads to it except turning wholly to Allah, dealing with Him alone, and preferring His pleasure over everything.'"

Indeed, the traveler on this path, if he misses his share of this world, has attained the lofty share that never escapes him. If the servant attains it, he attains everything; if he misses it, he misses everything. And if he attains his share of this world, he obtains it in the most agreeable manner. There is nothing more beneficial for the servant than these paths, nor any that brings him more surely to his pleasure, joy, and happiness. And success is from Allah.

[Section: Endurance/Permanence (al-Baqa')]

The Shaykh said: (Chapter on Permanence). God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And God is better and more enduring﴾ [Ta-Ha: 73].

The permanence (al-baqa') to which the Sufis (al-qawm) refer is a attribute of the servant and his station. The permanence in the verse is the permanence of the Lord and the continuance of His existence. The believing sorcerers mentioned it in this place because the enemy of God, Pharaoh, threatened them for believing with the destruction of their lives and the annihilation of their selves. So they said to him: "Whatever you do, that in which we have believed, and by which we have passed from your servitude to His servitude, and from seeking your pleasure and your station with you to seeking His pleasure and His station with Him, is better than you and more lasting. Your punishment and your bliss come to an end and cease, whereas His punishment, His bliss and His honour never end and never perish. How then should we prefer the ending, perishing, lowest, over the lasting, enduring, highest?"

But the point of allusion in the verse is that means, attachments, love and will follow their ends, their beloved and their objects of desire. Whoever's ultimate love and will is transient, his attachment ends when that ends, and his work, his striving, departs and vanishes. Whoever's object of seeking and ultimate end is lasting and permanent, without cessation or annihilation, and does not vanish or come to nothing, his attachment and his bliss in it endure with its enduring. Thus means follow ends, attachments follow what they attach to, and love follows the beloved. The beloved who perishes, vanishes and passes away is not like the beloved of whom "every thing is perishing except His Face" (Qur'an 28:88). The lover remains by the permanence of his beloved, is honoured by his honour, his worth is magnified according to his beloved, he is enriched by his richness, strengthened by his strength, exalted by his exaltation, and his standing is magnified in souls through serving Him, willing Him and loving Him. By God, were it not for the veil of heedlessness, habits, desire and transgressions, the heart would taste the greatest pain in attaching itself to other than the First Beloved, and would taste the greatest pleasure and joy in attaching itself to Him. So God is the one sought for help.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 20, verses 83–84:

Al-Daqqaq said, regarding Musa's words ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾:

He said: Its meaning is "out of longing for You." So he concealed it under the wording of "being pleased."

It is also said: Shu'ayb wept until his sight was lost. Allah revealed to him: "If this is for the sake of Paradise, I have permitted it to you; and if it is for the sake of the Fire, I have granted you protection from it." He said: "No, rather out of longing for You." Some of the gnostics ('arifin) said: "Whoever longs for Allah, everything longs for him."

Some of them said: The hearts of those who long are illuminated by the light of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. When their longing stirs, the light fills what lies between the heaven and the earth. Then Allah displays them to the angels and says: "These are the ones who long for Me. I call you to witness that I long for them more." If longing (shawq) is the journey of the heart in pursuit of its beloved and its yearning toward him, then it is among the most noble, exalted and lofty stations of the servants. Whoever denies the servant's longing for his Lord has denied his love for Him, because love necessarily entails longing. The lover is always longing for the meeting with his beloved: his heart finds no rest and his resolve is not settled except by reaching him.

(Section)

If you said, "Step into the Fire, and I will know that it is pleasing to you, or that it brings us near to your union,"
I would have stepped forward with my foot and trod upon it,
as guidance from you to me, or as going astray from your going astray.

Let it be pleasant for you that I hold my palm upon my chest,
and that my eye trembles from fear of your departure.

And if it grieves me that you have touched me with some hurt,
it still delights me that I have crossed your mind.

Among the signs of sincere love is that the lover's joy is not complete except with his beloved, and as long as he is absent from him, his whole life is clouded.

We are in the fullest joy, but
joy is complete only with you.

The fault of our condition, O people of my affection,
is that you are absent while we are present.

And another said:

Whoever is pleased by the new festival,
has lost its joy by it.

My joy would be complete
if my beloveds were present.

If the lover were asked at all times what he wishes for, he would say: the meeting with the beloved.

When we alighted at a place the dew had moistened,
graceful, and a garden of light, verdant,

I found in it the goodness of the place and its beauty,
so I wished, and you were my wishes.

Al-Junayd said: I heard al-Sarri say: "Longing is the most exalted station of the gnostic when it is realized in him; and when he is realized in longing, it diverts him from everything that preoccupies him, from the one he longs for."

It was also said: Allah, the Exalted, revealed to Dawud, peace be upon him: "Why do the young men of the Children of Israel occupy their souls with other than Me, while I long for them? What is this estrangement? If those who turn away from Me knew how I wait for them, how gentle I am with them, and how I love them to abandon their sins, they would die of longing for Me, and their joints would be severed by My love. This is My will for those who turn away from Me; so what is My will for those who turn toward Me?"

Al-Junayd was asked: From what does the lover weep when he meets the beloved? He said: "It is only out of joy in him and ecstasy from the intensity of longing for him."

He said: It has reached me that two brothers embraced, and one of them said, "Oh, my longing!" and the other said, "Oh, my ecstasy!"

(Section)

Al-Qushayri said: I heard our teacher Abu 'Ali al-Daqqaq distinguish between shawq and ishtiyaq, saying: "Shawq is calmed by meeting. Ishtiyaq is not removed by meeting." He said: And in its meaning they recited:

The eye does not turn away from him when it sees him,
until the eye returns to him, longing.

Al-Nasrabadhi said: For all creatures there is the station of shawq, but there is no station of ishtiyaq for them. Whoever enters the state of ishtiyaq is bewildered in it until no trace of him is seen in it and he has no settled place.

Al-Daqqaq said, regarding Musa's words ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84]:

He said: Its meaning is "out of longing for You." So he concealed it under the wording of "being pleased."

It is also said: The people of longing for the meeting with Allah sip the sweetness of nearness when it arrives, because of what has been unveiled to them of the spirit of arrival, which is sweeter than honey. So they are in the greatest delight and sweetness during its intoxication.

It is also said: Whoever longs for Allah, everything longs for him. As one of them said: "I enter into longing, while things long for me, and I withdraw from all of them."

On this it was said:

When the horses long for the watering places, they turn away from the water,
and then the watering places long for them.

There was an old woman whose husband was absent. Her husband returned from a journey. His family and relatives rejoiced at him, but she sat weeping. She was asked: "What makes you weep?"

She said: "The arrival of this young man reminded me of the day of arrival before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

O you who complained of longing because of the length of separation,
be patient, for perhaps tomorrow you will meet the one you love.

It is also said: Dawud, peace be upon him, once went out alone into the desert. Allah, the Exalted, revealed to him: "Why do I see you alone?" He said: "My God, my longing for Your meeting has taken hold of my heart, so it has come between me and the company of creatures." He said: "Return to them, for if you bring Me a runaway slave, I shall record you in the Preserved Tablet as a man of wisdom."

(Benefit)

In Tariq al-Hijratayn he said:

The matter of longing has already been discussed in full. Fleeing from the other and the opposite is not longing itself; rather, here there is something fled from and something fled toward. Longing is the journey of the heart toward the beloved, and this is not complete except by fleeing from its opposite. So longing is not the very act of fleeing from the traces and marks.

(Admonition)

Longing for Allah and for His meeting is a breeze that blows over the heart and cools it from the blaze of this world. Whoever settles his heart with his Lord finds calm and rest, and whoever sends it among people is agitated, and anxiety intensifies within him. The love of Allah does not enter a heart in which there is love of this world, except as a camel enters the eye of a needle.

When Allah loves a servant, He makes him His own, chooses him for His love, and singles him out for His worship. He occupies his concern with Him, his tongue with His remembrance, and his limbs with His service. The heart falls ill as the body falls ill, and its cure is in repentance and discipline. It rusts as a mirror rusts, and its polish is through remembrance. It becomes naked as the body becomes naked, and its adornment is piety. It hungers and thirsts as the body hungers, and its food and drink are knowledge, love, reliance, turning back (to Allah), and service. Beware of heedlessness toward the One who has set a term for your life and a limit for your days and breaths. Everything other than Him must be left; there is no escape from this. Among that is abandoning choice and planning in seeking an increase of worldly wealth, status, or in fear of loss, or in escaping an enemy, out of reliance on Allah and trust in His planning for you and His good choice for you. Then he lays his cheek before Him, surrenders the matter to Him, and is pleased with what He decrees for him, and he finds rest from worries, griefs and sorrows.

Whoever refuses except to plan for himself falls into distress, fatigue, bad condition and exhaustion. There is then no life that is clear, no heart that rejoices, no deed that grows, no hope that stands, and no rest that lasts. Allah, glorified is He, made the path to Himself easy for His creatures, and He veiled them from Him by their planning. Whoever is pleased with Allah's planning for him, settles into His choice, and submits to His judgment, Allah removes that veil; the heart then reaches out to its Lord and is at peace with Him. The one who relies (upon Allah) asks no one but Allah, does not object to Allah, and does not reserve anything with Allah. Whoever is preoccupied with himself is distracted from others, and whoever is preoccupied with his Lord is distracted from himself.

[Section: Restlessness (qalaq)]

This longing may grow strong and strip itself of patience, and then it is called qalaq (restlessness). The author of al-Manazil named it so and cited as evidence the words of Allah, the Exalted, relating the words of His interlocutor Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾.

It is as if he understood that Musa's haste was driven only by restlessness, which is the stripping of longing for the meeting and its appointed time.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that what drove Musa to haste was seeking his Lord's pleasure, and that His pleasure lies in hastening to His commands and rushing toward them.

For this reason the early scholars (al-salaf) used this verse as evidence that prayer at the beginning of its time is more excellent. I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah mention this. He said: The Lord's pleasure lies in hastening to His commands.

Then the author of al-Manazil defined it as the stripping of longing by removing patience, that is, its purification from every impurity such that patience falls away with it. If patience accompanies it, then it is longing (shawq).

Then Allah displays them to the angels and says: "These are the ones who long for Me. I call you to witness that I long for them more." If longing (shawq) is the journey of the heart in pursuit of its beloved and its yearning toward him, then it is among the most noble, exalted and lofty stations of the servants. Whoever denies the servant's longing for his Lord has denied his love for Him, because love necessarily entails longing. The lover is always longing for the meeting with his beloved: his heart finds no rest and his resolve is not settled except by reaching him.

(Section)

If you said, "Step into the Fire, and I will know that it is pleasing to you, or that it brings us near to your union,"
I would have stepped forward with my foot and trod upon it,

Let it be pleasant for you that I hold my palm upon my chest,
and that my eye trembles from fear of your departure.

And if it grieves me that you have touched me with some hurt,

We are in the fullest joy, but

My joy would be complete

[Section: Restlessness (qalaq)]

This longing may grow strong and strip itself of patience, and then it is called qalaq (restlessness). The author of al-Manazil named it so and cited as evidence the words of Allah, the Exalted, relating the words of His interlocutor Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾.

It is as if he understood that Musa's haste was driven only by restlessness, which is the stripping of longing for the meeting and its appointed time.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that what drove Musa to haste was seeking his Lord's pleasure, and that His pleasure lies in hastening to His commands and rushing toward them.

For this reason the early scholars (al-salaf) used this verse as evidence that prayer at the beginning of its time is more excellent. I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah mention this. He said: The Lord's pleasure lies in hastening to His commands.

Then the author of al-Manazil defined it as the stripping of longing by removing patience, that is, its purification from every impurity such that patience falls away with it. If patience accompanies it, then it is longing (shawq).

This is among the most vile of Satan's deceptions toward them.

Consider these people: how they took as a god something fashioned from earthly matter, which is found beneath the dust, needing to be smelted in fire and refined to purge its impurity, pounded with iron hammers, turned in the fire again and again, carved with files, and whose maker gave it a form and shape resembling the animal known for dullness, humiliation and subjugation.

Yet they made it the god of Moses, and attributed to him error, since he went seeking another god.
