We worship Him by His command and His decree, and we rely on Him in executing His command by His decree. This is the reality of knowledge, and the possessor of this station is the gnostic of Allah. Upon this all the messengers agreed, from the first to the last.

As for the one who says:
"I have become one acted upon by what He chooses from me, so my every act is obedience,"
and who says: "Even if I disobey His command, I have obeyed His will and His wish," and who says: "The gnostic does not forbid wrongdoing, because of his insight into Allah's secret in predestination," such a person has departed from what all the messengers were upon, and he is not among their followers. Allah, glorified is He, related the argument from predestination of the polytheists, the enemies of the messengers, saying: ﴿Those who associated partners with Allah will say: "Had Allah willed, we would not have associated, nor would our fathers"﴾ up to His words: ﴿Say: "Then to Allah belongs the conclusive proof. So had He willed, He would have guided you all."﴾ And He said: ﴿Those who associated partners said: "Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, we or our fathers"﴾ up to His words: ﴿So is there upon the messengers except clear notification?﴾ And He said: ﴿And when it is said to them: "Spend from what Allah has provided you," those who disbelieved say to those who believed: "Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed?"﴾ And He said: ﴿And they say: "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them." They have no knowledge of that; they only guess.﴾

These are four places in which the argument from predestination is related from His enemies. Their shaykh and imam in this was their most despicable enemy, Iblis, who argued against Allah by His decree, saying: ﴿He said: "My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them upon the earth and will mislead them all."﴾

If it is said: The texts and reason have established the truth of their words, "Had Allah willed, we would not have associated, nor our fathers," and "Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him," and "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them," for what Allah wills comes to be and what He does not will does not come to be. And the Most High said: ﴿And had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾, and He said: ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾.

Then how could I call them liars, when He denied them knowledge and affirmed that they were only guessing, while they are truthful in what they claim? All the People of the Sunnah say: If God willed, no polytheist would have associated partners with Him, no unbeliever would have disbelieved, and none of His creatures would have disobeyed Him. So how can what they claim be denied when it is true?

It is said: God denied them what they claimed to be the most lying and the most wicked of falsehoods. He did not deny them any truth or right. Rather, He denied them the most false of falsehoods. They did not mention what they mentioned in order to affirm His decree, His lordship, His oneness, their own need of Him, their reliance upon Him, and their seeking help from Him. Had they said it in that sense, they would have been correct. They said it only to oppose His law and to repel His command. Thus they opposed His law and command, and they rejected them by His decree and destiny. Everyone who opposes a command and rejects it by appealing to destiny agrees with them in this.

Furthermore, they argued from His general will and decree to His love for what He wills, His approval of it, and His permission for it. Thus they combined several kinds of error: opposing the command with destiny, repelling it by destiny, and reporting about God that He loves this from them and approves of it, since He willed and decreed it, and that they have a proof against the messengers through decree and destiny. Groups of people who claim realization and gnosis, or who claim it falsely, have inherited this error from them and followed them in it. They say: when the gnostic witnesses the divine judgment, blame falls away from him.

The words of Shaykh al-Islam Abu Isma'il Abdullah ibn Muhammad al-Ansari (may God have mercy on him) contain something that seems to suggest this, though God protects him from it. In the chapter on repentance in *Manazil al-sa'irin* (The Stations of Travelers), he said: "The subtleties of repentance are three.

The first: that we examine the offense and the decree, and recognize God's purpose in them: His letting you be and your committing them. God lets the servant and the sin alone for one of two reasons: that He may make His servant know His lesson in His decree, His goodness in His guidance, His forbearance in giving respite to the one who rides [sin], His generosity in accepting the servant's excuse, and His grace in forgiving him. The second is that He may establish against the servant the proof of His justice, so that He punishes him for his sin with His proof.

The second subtlety: to know that the seeking of the discerning sincere one does not leave him any good deed at all, since he travels between witnessing the favor (minnah) and seeking out the fault of the self and of the deed.

The third subtlety: the servant's witnessing of the judgment leaves him no appreciation of any good deed and no disapproval of any evil deed, because he has ascended from all meanings to the meaning of the judgment."

The apparent meaning of this last statement nullifies the appreciation of good and the disapproval of evil, yet all the sacred laws rest on the appreciation of this and the disapproval of that. Rather, witnessing the judgment increases the discerning one's appreciation of good and disapproval of evil. The more his knowledge of God, His names, His attributes, and His command grows, the stronger his appreciation and disapproval become, because in this he agrees with his Lord and His messengers, and with what the Most Beautiful Names and the Exalted Attributes require. Shaykh al-Islam was in this agreeing with the command, and his anger for God, for His limits, and for His prohibitions is well known among the elite and the common people. His earlier words clearly show the firmness of his stance in disapproving what God disapproved and approving what God approved. His words are clear (muhkam) in this, and this statement is ambiguous (mutashabih), so it must be referred back to his clear words.

What fits him best is what our shaykh Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Wasiti said in his commentary. He mentioned a principle concerning *fana'* (annihilation) and *istilam* (obliteration). He said: "Fana' is an expression for the servant's being overwhelmed (istilam) by the dominance of the Real's existence and the strength of the knowledge of Him in the servant. Through this his certainty and knowledge of Him and of His attributes increase, so he becomes stunned, just as a person is stunned by a great matter that has overtaken him. He may be absent from awareness of the important matters that overtook him, as when a man stands before a great, overpowering sovereign of the kings of the earth, and what he observes of the sovereign's awe and power distracts him from much of what he perceives. This is an approximation, and the reality is beyond it. How then about one whom God, the Mighty and Majestic, has made to witness His singularity (fardaniyyah), when there was nothing with Him? He sees things as dead, having no subsistence except through His power, and he witnesses them as an imagination, like dust, in relation to the existence of the Real, exalted is He. This occurs in the inner insight of the heart through sound unveiling, after purification and training in bearing the burdens of the Law, taking on its loads and adopting its character. God purifies His servant from his filth and unveils to his heart, so he sees the realities of things. When the lights of real, spiritual witnessing that indicate the greatness of singularity manifest upon the servant, the existence that belongs to the servant vanishes and dissolves, just as the night disappears when the morning brightens. The servant, in that state, eats and drinks, and nothing appears on him that differs from what he is accustomed to. Yet his faith and certainty increase, until his faith may cover everything in his heart during moments of intoxication (sukr). His existence remains like an imagination, standing in servanthood in the presence of the Lord of Majesty. Sound insights return to him in knowing things when he becomes sober (sahw). Then the lack of discernment (tamyiz) leaves him, and he becomes strong in his state and acts. This is *baqa'* (subsistence), by which he acts upon things, and what he found of faith and certainty in the state of subsistence is not veiled from him. Rather, his first awareness returns to him, with another existence that God, the Mighty and Majestic, takes charge of, and his witnessing of it is that God's standing over him is by His management. He reaches the station of the one who is willed (murad) after passing the station of the seeker (murid), so by Him he hears and by Him he speaks, as in the authentic hadith.

"Another aspect: the one who is annihilated in his state of fana', before he reaches subsistence, sobriety, and discernment, has his heart's place of asceticism (zuhd), patience (sabr), and scrupulousness (wara') covered over. This does not mean that those stations have gone and the servant has been lifted from them. It means that witnessing has covered their place in the heart, and they are folded and absorbed within what he has found, as a lower state is absorbed into a higher one. They become implicit and subordinate to what the finder has found of the existence of the Real. The heart becomes occupied with the higher state rather than the lower one. So if the servant's heart were searched, one would find within it asceticism, scrupulousness, and the realities of fear and hope hidden beneath mountain-like existential states, so that the heart cannot contain them all together. In the state of subsistence, sobriety, and discernment, those stations return to him through God, not through his own existence.

"If you know this, the problem in his statement that witnessing does not leave the servant any appreciation of a good deed or disapproval of an evil deed, because he has ascended to the meaning of the judgment, is resolved. That is, the attribute of God's judgment fills his insight and occupies it. He witnesses God's standing over things, His management of them, and His judgment upon them. He sees all things issuing from Him through the execution of His judgment, His decree, and His will in creation. Through his observation of this unity (jam'), he becomes absent from discernment (tamyiz) and distinction (farq). This is called *jam'* because the servant's gaze gathers upon his Master in every judgment that occurs in the cosmos. In contemplating this judgment from which the actions proceed, his heart gathers. Because his heart is weak at this gathering, it cannot contain the legal discernment between good and evil. That is, the judgment of his knowledge of good and evil is folded within this knowledge, which veils him from discernment. This does not mean that the judgment of approving and disapproving has been removed from his heart. Rather, it has been absorbed into his witnessing and folded within it, so that if one searched, one would find the judgment of approval and disapproval hidden within that witnessing." And success is from God.

The summary of what our shaykh (may God have mercy on him) mentioned is this: the act has two aspects. One aspect subsists in the Lord, the Exalted, namely His decree, His destiny, and His knowledge of it. The servant has two observations: an observation of the first aspect and an observation of the second. The perfection is that he is not absent from one observation by the other. Rather, he witnesses the Lord's decree, destiny, and will, and at the same time witnesses his own act, his sin, and his obedience or disobedience. Thus he witnesses both lordship and servanthood, and in his heart the meaning of God's words ﴿for whoever among you wills to be upright﴾ combines with His words ﴿And you will not, except that God wills﴾, and His words ﴿Indeed, it is a reminder, so whoever wills may remember it. And they will not remember, except that God wills﴾. Some people have hearts wide enough to contain these two witnessings. Others have hearts too narrow to combine them, because of the strength of what descends upon them and the weakness of the receptacle. Such a person is absent, through witnessing servanthood, acquisition (kasb), and the aspect of obedience and disobedience, from witnessing the judgment that subsists in the Lord, the Exalted, without denying it. Only the trace of the act and its legal judgment appears to him. This does not harm him as long as belief in the judgment remains established in his heart. Others are absent through witnessing the judgment, its precedence, and God's priority and precedence over things, away from the aspect of their own servanthood, acquisition, obedience, and disobedience. Through witnessing the judgment, they are absent from the one judged by it, let alone its attribute. When he does not witness the act itself, how could he witness it as good or evil? This also does not harm him, provided that his knowledge of the goodness and evil of the act remains in his heart. It is only hidden from him because the witnessing of the judgment has overpowered his heart. And success is from God.

How far is this from the argument of God's enemies, who use His will and decree to annul His command and prohibition? Their worshippers, these unbelievers, witness all their acts as acts of obedience, because they conform to the prior will. Yet if someone else angers them and falls short of their rights, they do not witness his act as obedience, even though it too conforms to the will. Whoever argues from destiny to nullify the command and prohibition is among the most ignorant and unjust of people, and the most devoted to his own desire. Reflect on His words, exalted is He, after relating what His enemies said, arguing with His will and decree to nullify what His messenger commanded them, and that were it not for His love and approval of it, He would not have willed it from them: ﴿Say: To God belongs the conclusive proof. So if He had willed, He would have guided you all﴾. He reports that the proof belongs to Him against them, through His messengers, His books, the clarification of what benefits and harms them, and His enabling them to believe by knowing His commands and prohibitions. He gave them hearing, sight, and intellect. Thus His conclusive proof is established against them, and their false proof against Him, through His will and decree, collapses. Then He confirmed the completeness of the proof with His words: ﴿So if He had willed, He would have guided you all﴾.

This implies that He alone is singular in lordship, dominion, and management of His creation, that there is no lord but Him and no god besides Him. How, then, could they worship another god along with Him? Affirming destiny and will is therefore part of His conclusive proof against them, and that all affairs belong to God, and that everything other than God is void. Destiny, decree, and the executing will are among the greatest proofs of monotheism. But the wrongdoers and deniers made them a proof for their polytheism. So God's proof is the conclusive one, and theirs is the refuted one. And success is from God.

Knowing this, Moses was too knowledgeable of God, His names, and His attributes to blame a man for a sin he repented of, after which his Lord chose him, guided him, and selected him. And Adam knew his Lord too well to argue from His decree and destiny for his disobedience. Rather, Moses only blamed Adam for the disobedience that reached his descendants when they were expelled from the Garden and sent down to the abode of trial and affliction, because of their father's error. Mentioning the error was a reminder of the cause of the calamity and affliction that befell the descendants. This is why Moses said to him, "You expelled us and yourself from the Garden," and in another wording, "You made us miserable."

So Adam argued from destiny against the calamity. He said that this calamity that befell the descendants because of my error had been written in His decree before I was created. Destiny may be invoked for calamities, but not for sins. That is: Would you blame me for a calamity that was decreed for me and for you before I was created, by so many years? This is the answer of our shaykh (may God have mercy on him). Another answer may also be suggested: arguing from destiny for a sin is beneficial in one situation and harmful in another. It is beneficial when one argues with it after the sin has occurred, and repents from it, and abandons repeating it, as Adam did. Then mentioning destiny at that point is part of monotheism and the knowledge of the Lord's names and attributes, and mentioning it benefits the one who recalls it and the one who hears it. It does not repel a command or a prohibition, nor does it annul the Law. Rather, it reports the pure truth in the manner of monotheism and disavowal of one's own power and strength.

This is clarified by the fact that Adam said to Moses, "Do you blame me for doing an act that was written against me before I was created?" When a man sins, then repents, and the matter is ended so that it is as though it had not happened, and then someone rebukes him and blames him for it, it is acceptable for him to argue from destiny afterward, saying, "This was a matter decreed against me before I was created." He has not used destiny to repel a right, nor mentioned it as a proof for falsehood, and there is no harm in arguing with it. The situation in which arguing with it is harmful is the present and the future: when one commits a forbidden act or abandons an obligation, and someone blames him for it, and he argues from destiny to justify it and persist in it. Then he annuls a right by this argument and commits falsehood, as those who insisted on their polytheism and worship of other than God argued, saying: ﴿If God had willed, we would not have associated, nor would our fathers﴾, and ﴿If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾. They argued with it, justifying what they were doing, and they did not repent of their act, nor resolve to abandon it, nor acknowledge its corruption. This is the opposite of one who has realized the error of his own self, repented, and resolved with all determination never to return. If someone later blames him, he says, "What happened was by God's decree."

The crux of the matter is this: when blame is lifted, arguing from destiny is valid. When blame is actually present, arguing from destiny is invalid.

If it is said: Ali argued from destiny for abandoning night prayer, and the Prophet (ﷺ) approved it, as is in the authentic report from Ali: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to him and Fatimah at night and said to them, 'Will you not pray?' I said, 'O Messenger of God, our souls are in the hand of God. If He wills to raise them, He raises them.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) turned away when I said that and did not reply to me. Then I heard him as he was leaving, striking his thigh and saying: ﴿And man is ever most disputatious﴾."

It is answered: Ali did not argue from destiny to abandon an obligation or to commit a forbidden act. He only said that his soul and Fatimah's soul were in God's hand, so if He willed to wake them and raise their souls, He would raise them. This agrees with the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying on the night they slept in the valley: "God took our souls where He willed and returned them where He willed." This is a sound argument, and whoever makes it is excused, because the sleeper is not negligent. Arguing from destiny by one who is not negligent is valid. The Prophet (ﷺ) guided toward arguing from destiny in the situation where it benefits the servant. Muslim related in his Sahih from Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, "The strong believer is better and more beloved to God than the weak believer. In everything there is good. Be eager for what benefits you, seek help from God, and do not be incapable. If something befalls you, do not say, 'If only I had done such and such.' Rather, say, 'God decreed it, and He does what He wills,' for 'if only' opens the work of Satan."

This noble hadith contains great principles of faith. The first: God, glorified and exalted, is described as loving, and He truly loves. The second: He loves what the requirements of His names and attributes call for, and what agrees with them. He is the Strong, so He loves the strong believer. He is One and loves oneness (witr). He is Beautiful and loves beauty. He is Knowing and loves the knowledgeable. He is Pure and loves purity. He is Faithful and loves the faithful. He is the Doer of good and loves the doers of good. He is the Patient and loves the patient. He is the Grateful and loves the grateful.

Another principle: His love for believers varies, so He loves some of them more than others.

Another: a person's happiness lies in being eager for what benefits him in his livelihood and his hereafter. Eagerness is exerting effort and expending one's capacity. When the eager person hits upon what benefits him, his eagerness is praiseworthy. His perfection lies in combining two things: that he be eager, and that his eagerness be for what benefits him. If someone is eager for what does not benefit him, or does what benefits him without eagerness, he loses perfection in proportion to what he has missed. So all good lies in being eager for what benefits. Since a person's eagerness and actions occur only by God's help, will, and enabling, He commanded him to seek His help, so that the station of ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ would be fulfilled in him. His eagerness for what benefits him is worship of God, and it is not complete except by His help. So He commanded him to worship Him and seek His help. Then He said, "Do not be incapable," because incapacity contradicts eagerness for what benefits him and contradicts seeking God's help. The one who is eager for what benefits him and seeks God's help is the opposite of the incapable. This is guidance before the decreed matter returns to what is among the greatest causes of its attainment, which is eagerness for it together with seeking help from the One in whose hand are the reins of affairs, from whom they proceed and to whom they return.

If something he was not decreed to obtain escapes him, he has two states. One is incapacity, which is the key to Satan's work. Incapacity leads him to "if only," and there is no benefit in "if only" here. It is rather the key to blame, distress, anger, regret, grief, and all of that is Satan's work. So the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade him to begin his work with this key, and commanded him to the second state, which is to look at destiny and observe it: that if it had been decreed for him, it would not have escaped him, and no one could have overpowered him in it. So there is nothing more beneficial for him here than witnessing destiny and the Lord's executing will, which necessitates the existence of what is decreed. When that will is absent, the existence of the decreed matter is impossible. This is why he said, "If something overcomes you, do not say, 'If only I had done such and such, it would have been so,' but say, 'God decreed it, and He does what He wills.'" Thus he guided him to what benefits him in both states: the state of attaining what he sought, and the state of its loss. Therefore this hadith is one that the servant can never do without. Rather, it is the most necessary thing for him. It contains the affirmation of destiny, acquisition, choice, standing, and servanthood, outwardly and inwardly, in both the state of attaining the desired thing and the state of its absence. And success is from God.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 20, verse 124 (part 1 of 3):

His turning away from His remembrance includes his turning away from the Reminder that He sent down, which is that he does not remember the One who sent it down in His Book. This is the meaning of his turning away from remembering his Lord through His Book, His names, His attributes, His commands, His signs, and His blessings and favours. All of these are consequences of turning away from the Book of his Lord, the Exalted. He turns away from My Book: he does not recite it, does not reflect upon it, does not act by it, and does not understand it. His life and his livelihood will only be constricted for him, distressed, and he will be punished within them.

Al-ḍank (ضنك) means narrowness, hardship, and affliction.

Describing the livelihood itself as ḍank is an intensification (mubālagha). This livelihood has been interpreted as the punishment of the barzakh (the intermediate realm between death and resurrection), but the correct view is that it encompasses his livelihood in this world and his condition in the barzakh. He will be in ḍank in both abodes, meaning hardship, toil, and constriction.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in Madarij al-Salikin (Stations of the Wayfarers):

"The livelihood that is ḍank has been interpreted as the punishment of the grave. The correct view is that it is in this world and in the barzakh. Whoever turns away from His Reminder that He sent down will have constriction of the chest, distress in life, abundant fear, intense greed and fatigue for the world, and grief over its loss before he obtains it and after he obtains it. There are also pains within all of this that the heart does not perceive because of its intoxication and its immersion in drunkenness. He does not awaken for a moment without feeling and perceiving this pain, so he hastens to remove it with a second intoxication. He remains like this for the duration of his life. And what livelihood could be narrower than this, if the heart had any awareness?

The hearts of the people of innovation, of those who turn away from the Qur'an, of the heedless of Allah, and of the people of sin are in a hell before the Greatest Hell, while the hearts of the righteous are in a bliss before the Greatest Bliss: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, and indeed the wicked will be in hellfire﴾ [al-Infitar: 13]. This is in their three abodes. It is not exclusive to the Hereafter, although its completion, perfection, and manifestation is in the Hereafter. In the barzakh it is less than that, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And indeed for those who do wrong there is a punishment short of that﴾ [al-Tur: 47]. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They say, 'When is this promise, if you are truthful?' Say, 'Perhaps some of what you are hastening will be right behind you'﴾ [al-Naml: 71].

In this world it is less than what is in the barzakh, but the immersion in the intoxication of desires, casting that aside from the heart, and not reflecting upon it prevents one from perceiving it.

A servant may suffer a physical pain, so he casts it from his heart, cuts off his attention from it, and directs his focus to something else so that he does not feel it at all. If that attention were removed from him, he would cry out from the intensity of the pain. So what is the assumption regarding the punishment of the hearts and their pains?"

(Benefit)
Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah guarantees that whoever recites the Qur'an and acts by what is in it will not go astray in this world nor be miserable in the Hereafter." Then he recited this verse.

His words, ﴿Whoever turns away from My remembrance﴾, encompass the Reminder that He sent down, which is the guidance that the messengers brought. The context of the discussion indicates this, in His words: ﴿Thus Our signs came to you, but you forgot them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 126].

This is the turning away from His remembrance. If this is the condition of one who turns away from it, what is the condition of one who opposes it with his intellect, or with the intellect of one he has imitated and thought well of? Just as one is not a believer unless he accepts it and submits to it, whoever turns away from it and opposes it is among the furthest of people from faith in it.

(Subtlety)
His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed for him is a livelihood of ḍank, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾.

He described him with blindness, which is the opposite of guidance, and with a livelihood of ḍank, which is the opposite of happiness. The Book of Allah begins with guidance and ends with happiness, while the speech of those who oppose it with their intellects begins with misguidance and ends with wretchedness.

(Section)
When He, glory be to Him, informed about the condition of those who follow His guidance, and what they have of abundance and goodness of life in their livelihood and their return, He then informed about the condition of those who turn away from guidance and do not follow it. He said: ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed for him is a livelihood of ḍank﴾. That is, from the Reminder that I sent down. Here, "remembrance" (dhikr) is a verbal noun annexed to its agent, like "my standing" and "my recitation", not annexed to its object. The meaning is not "whoever turns away from being remembered by Me", but this is a necessary implication and consequence of it from another angle, which we will mention.

A better view than this is that one says: "remembrance" here is annexed by idafat al-asma' (nominal annexation), not the annexation of verbal nouns to their objects of action.

The meaning is: whoever turns away from My Book and does not follow it. The Qur'an is called a reminder (dhikr). Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anbiya': 50]. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿That, We recite it to you from the signs and the wise reminder﴾ [Al 'Imran: 58]. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And it is not but a reminder for the worlds﴾ [Sad: 87]. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved in the reminder when it came to them, and indeed it is a mighty Book﴾ [Fussilat: 41]. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿You can only warn one who follows the reminder and fears the Most Merciful unseen﴾ [Ya-Sin: 11]. Examples of this are many.

So its annexation is like the annexation of the solid nouns whose purpose is the annexation of the operator to its object.

Its parallel in the annexation of the active participle is His words: ﴿Forgiver of sin, Accepter of repentance, Severe in penalty﴾ [Ghafir: 3]. These annexations are not intended to express a renewed act, but are intended to express a fixed, inherent attribute. For this reason they occur as attributes of the most definite of definites, which is the name of Allah, the Exalted, in His words: ﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Knowing, Forgiver of sin, Accepter of repentance, Severe in penalty, Owner of bounty. There is no deity except Him; to Him is the final return﴾ [Ghafir: 2-3].

(Section)
The livelihood of ḍank has been interpreted as the punishment of the grave. There is no doubt that it is part of the livelihood of ḍank, but the verse encompasses something more general than that. Although it is indefinite in an affirmative context, its generality is in meaning, since He, glory be to Him, attached the livelihood of ḍank to turning away from His remembrance. The one who turns away from it has a share of the narrowness of livelihood in proportion to his turning away. Even if he enjoys all kinds of blessings in this world, in his heart there is loneliness, humiliation, and regrets that cut hearts, false hopes, and the punishment that is present within him. What hides this from him is the intoxications of desires, love of passion, love of the world, and leadership. Even if the intoxication of wine is not added to that, the intoxication of these matters is greater than the intoxication of wine, for its possessor may recover and become sober, but the intoxication of whims and love of the world does not leave its possessor sober unless he is among the army of the dead. So the livelihood of ḍank is necessary for whoever turns away from the remembrance of Allah, which He sent down to His Messenger (ﷺ), in his life in this world, in the barzakh, and on the day of his return. His eye will not be cooled, his heart will not be calm, and his soul will not be at rest, except with its God and object of worship who is the truth, while every object of worship other than Him is falsehood. Whoever's eye is cooled by Allah, every eye will be cooled by him. Whoever's eye is not cooled by Allah, his soul will be torn apart by regrets over the world. Allah, the Exalted, has only made the good life for those who believe in Him and do righteous deeds, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 97].

So He guaranteed for the people of faith and righteous deeds reward in this world through a good life, and the best reward on the Day of Resurrection. So they have the best of both lives, and they are living in both abodes.

(Another section)
His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Indeed, for him is a livelihood of ḍank﴾ were interpreted by more than one of the early generations (salaf) as the punishment of the grave. They considered this verse to be one of the proofs indicating the punishment of the grave. For this reason He said: ﴿We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind.﴾ He said: ﴿My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, while I was seeing?﴾ He said: ﴿Thus Our signs came to you, but you forgot them, and likewise today you are forgotten﴾ [Ta-Ha: 125-126].

That is, you will be left in punishment, just as you left acting upon Our signs. So He mentioned the punishment of the barzakh and the punishment of the abode of destruction.

Its parallel is His, the Exalted's, words regarding the people of Pharaoh: ﴿The Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. This is in the barzakh. And: ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established: Admit the people of Pharaoh into the most severe punishment﴾ [Ghafir: 46]. This is the greatest resurrection.

Its parallel is His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, and the angels are extending their hands: "Release your souls. Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation for what you used to say about Allah other than the truth, and you were arrogant toward His signs"﴾ [al-An'am: 93]. So the angels' saying "Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation" refers to the punishment of the barzakh, which begins with the day of seizing and death.

Its parallel is His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿If only you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs: "Taste the punishment of the burning"﴾ [al-Anfal: 50].

This tasting is in the barzakh, and its beginning is at the time of death, for it is joined to His words: ﴿striking their faces and their backs﴾, and it is from the speech that is omitted, its statement being indicated by the context, like its parallels.

Both occur at the time of death. In the authentic (sahih) collections, from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib (may Allah be pleased with him), regarding His words: ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾ [Ibrahim: 27], he said: "It was revealed concerning the punishment of the grave." The reports about the punishment of the grave nearly reach the level of being mass-transmitted (mutawatir).

The intended point is that Allah, glory be to Him, informed that whoever turns away from His remembrance, which is the guidance that whoever follows will not go astray nor be miserable, then for him is a livelihood of ḍank. He guaranteed for whoever keeps His covenant that He will give him a good life and will reward him in the Hereafter. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life. And We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾.

So He informed about the success of whoever adheres to His covenant in knowledge and action: in the immediate life, a good life, and in the Hereafter, the best reward. This is the opposite of the one who has a livelihood of ḍank in this world and in the barzakh, and whom He forgets in punishment in the Hereafter.

He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And whoever turns blind to the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he is his companion. And indeed they hinder them from the path while they think they are guided﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36-37].

So He informed that whoever is afflicted with a devil as his companion, and his misguidance through him, is only because of his turning away and blindness toward His remembrance that He sent down to His Messenger. So the punishment for this turning away was that He appointed for him a devil to accompany him, who hinders him from the path of his Lord and the way of his success.

He thinks he is guided, until when he reaches his Lord on the Day of Resurrection together with his companion, and sees his destruction and bankruptcy, he says: ﴿Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts! Wretched is the companion﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 38].

Everyone who turns away from being guided by the revelation, which is the remembrance of Allah, will inevitably say this on the Day of Resurrection.

If it is said: Is there an excuse for this person in his misguidance, since he thought he was on guidance, as He said: ﴿And they think they are guided﴾?

It is said: There is no excuse for this one, nor for those like him among the misguided, whose origin of misguidance is turning away from the revelation that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought, even if he thought he was guided. He is negligent by his turning away from following the caller to guidance. So if he goes astray, it is only because of his negligence and turning away.

This is different from one whose misguidance is due to the non-arrival of the message and his inability to reach it. That one has a different ruling. The threat in the Qur'an pertains only to the first.

As for the second, Allah does not punish anyone except after establishing the proof against him, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We would never punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15].

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Messengers as bringers of good tidings and warners, so that mankind will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa': 165].

He, the Exalted, said regarding the people of the Fire: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 76].

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Lest a soul should say: "Oh, my regret over what I neglected regarding Allah, and that I was indeed among the mockers," or say: "If only Allah had guided me, I would have been among the righteous," or say when it sees the punishment: "If only I had another return, so that I might be among the doers of good." Yes, My signs had come to you, but you denied them and were arrogant, and you were among the disbelievers﴾ [al-Zumar: 56-59].

This is abundant in the Qur'an.

(Section: The creation of the human body from the earth, and his soul from the realm of the heavens, and their conjunction)

When the body is hungry, sleepless, and engaged in service, the soul finds lightness and ease, longs for the place from which it was created, and yearns for its upper world. When the body is fed, pampered, given sleep, and occupied with its comfort and ease, it inclines toward the place from which it was created, and the soul is pulled along with it, so it becomes imprisoned. If it were not accustomed to the prison, it would cry out in pain and depart from it, separated from its upper world, as a tormented person cries out.

In sum, whenever the body is light, the soul becomes subtle and light, and seeks its upper world. Whenever the body is heavy and inclines toward desires and comfort, the soul becomes heavy and descends from its world, becoming earthly and lowly. So you see a man whose soul is in the highest companionship while his body is with you, so he is asleep on his bed while his soul is at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, circling around the Throne. And another standing in service with his body while his soul is in the lowest level, roaming among the lowest things. When the soul departs from the body, it joins its companion, either the highest or the lowest. In the highest companionship is every delight of the eye, every bliss, joy, gladness, pleasure, and good life. In the lowest companionship is every worry, grief, narrowness, sorrow, distressed life, and livelihood of ḍank. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed for him is a livelihood of ḍank﴾.

So His remembrance is His speech that He sent down to His Messenger, and turning away from it is abandoning its reflection and acting upon it. The livelihood of ḍank has been interpreted most commonly as the punishment of the grave, as said by Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and Ibn 'Abbas, and there is a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) about it. The root meaning of ḍank in the language is narrowness and hardship, and everything that is constricted is ḍank. It is said: a ḍank dwelling, and a ḍank life. So this livelihood of ḍank stands in contrast to expanding the soul and the body with desires, pleasures, and comfort. For the soul, whenever it is expanded for, it constricts the heart until the livelihood becomes ḍank. And whenever it is constricted, it expands the heart until it opens and becomes spacious. So the ḍank of livelihood in this world by the requirement of piety is its expansiveness in the barzakh and the Hereafter, and the expansiveness of livelihood in this world by the ruling of desire is its ḍank in the barzakh and the Hereafter. So choose the best and most pleasant and enduring of the two livelihoods, and afflict the body for the sake of the bliss of the soul, for the soul is not afflicted by the bliss of the body. The bliss and misery of the soul are greater and more enduring, while the bliss and misery of the body are shorter and lighter. And Allah is the One sought for help.

[Section: On the effects of sins]

Sins have bad, blameworthy effects that harm the heart and the body, in this world and in the Hereafter, which only Allah knows.

**Ibn al-Qayyim's Tafsir (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 20, verse 124 (part 2 of 3)**

Among its consequences is the deprivation of knowledge, for knowledge is a light that Allah casts into the heart, and sin extinguishes that light.

When al-Imam al-Shafi'i (Shafi'i) sat before Malik and recited to him, he was impressed by the abundance of his understanding, the brightness of his intelligence, and the completeness of his comprehension. So he said: "I see that Allah has placed a light upon your heart, so do not extinguish it with the darkness of disobedience."

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, also said:

*I complained to Waki' about the poor state of my memory,*
*So he guided me to abandon sins.*
*And he said: know that knowledge is a bounty,*
*And the bounty of Allah is not given to one who disobeys.*

Among its consequences is the deprivation of provision. In the Musnad there is the hadith: "Indeed, a servant is deprived of provision because of a sin he commits," which has already been mentioned. Just as piety (taqwa) is a means of attracting provision, abandoning piety is a means of attracting poverty. Allah's provision is never drawn in by anything like the abandonment of sins.

Among its consequences is a loneliness that the disobedient person finds in his heart between himself and Allah, which no pleasure can balance or equal at all. Even if all the pleasures of this world were gathered for him, they would not suffice to compensate for that loneliness. This is something only one whose heart is alive can feel, for a dead person does not feel pain from a wound. Therefore, if sins were abandoned only out of fear of falling into that loneliness, a rational person would be worthy of abandoning them.

A man complained to one of the knowers (al-'arifin) of a loneliness he found within himself, and he said to him:

*If sins have made you lonely,*
*Then leave them, if you wish, and seek intimacy.*

Nothing is more bitter upon the heart than the loneliness of sin following sin. So Allah is the One sought for help.

Among its consequences is the loneliness that arises between him and other people, especially the people of goodness among them. He finds a estrangement between himself and them, and the more this estrangement grows, the further he becomes from them and from sitting with them, and he is deprived of the blessing of benefiting from them, and he draws near to the party of Satan to the degree that he distances himself from the party of the Merciful. This loneliness grows until it becomes firmly established, so that it arises between him and his wife, his children, and his relatives, and between him and himself, so that you see him estranged even from himself.

Waki' also reported, saying: Zakariyya narrated to us from 'Amir, who said: 'A'isha wrote to Mu'awiya: "To proceed: when a servant acts in disobedience to Allah, the one who praises him among the people counts as a blamer."

Abu Nu'aym reported from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, from Abu al-Darda', who said: "Let a man beware lest the hearts of the believers curse him without his being aware." Then he said: "Do you know why this is?" I said: "No." He said: "A servant is alone with the disobedience of Allah, so Allah casts his hatred into the hearts of the believers without his being aware."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad mentioned in the Kitab al-Zuhd of his father, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, that when debt weighed upon him, he grieved over it and said: "I truly recognize this grief as the result of a sin I committed forty years ago."

**Sin may not have an immediate effect**

Here is a subtle point in which people err regarding sin: they do not see its effect immediately. Its effect may be delayed and forgotten, and the servant thinks that it will not leave any trace afterward, and that the matter is as the poet said:

*If a wall does not raise dust when it falls,*
*Then after its falling there is no dust.*

Glory be to Allah! How many creatures has this point destroyed? How much blessing has it wiped away? How much retribution has it brought? And how many are deceived by it, scholars and virtuous people included, let alone the ignorant? The one who is deceived does not know that sin strikes, even after a time, just as poison strikes, and just as a wound that has healed strikes again when it is hidden by rot and corruption.

Imam Ahmad reported from Abu al-Darda': "Worship Allah as though you see Him, count yourselves among the dead, and know that a little that suffices you is better than a lot that distracts you. Know that righteousness does not wear out, and that sin is not forgotten."

Some of the worshippers looked at a child and contemplated his beauty, and he was visited in his dream and told: "You will surely find its consequence after forty years."

This is in addition to the fact that sin has an immediate payment that does not lag behind it. Sulayman al-Taymi said: "A man commits a sin in secret, and in the morning he has its humiliation upon him."

Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi said: "I am astonished at a person of intellect who says in his supplication, 'O Allah, do not let my enemies rejoice over me,' and then he gives every enemy he has cause to rejoice over himself." It was said: "How is that?" He said: "He disobeys Allah, and on the Day of Resurrection every enemy rejoices over him."

Dhu al-Nun said: "Whoever betrays Allah in secret, Allah will expose his concealment openly."

One of the early generations (al-salaf) said: "I disobey Allah, and I see that in the temperament of my animal and my wife."

Among its consequences is the making of his affairs difficult for him. He turns to no matter without finding it closed before him or made difficult for him. This is like how whoever meets Allah in piety, Allah makes ease for him in his affairs, while whoever neglects piety, Allah makes hardship for him in his affairs. How strange, by Allah! How does a servant find the doors of goodness and benefit closed to him and their paths made difficult for him, while he does not know where he has been struck from?

Among its consequences is a darkness that he truly finds in his heart, which he senses just as one senses the darkness of a pitch-black night when it gathers. The darkness of disobedience becomes for his heart like sensory darkness for his sight, for obedience is light and disobedience is darkness. Whenever the darkness grows stronger, his bewilderment increases, until he falls into innovations, misguidance, and destructive matters while he is unaware, like a blind man taken out into the darkness of night who walks alone. This darkness grows until it appears in the eye, then grows until it covers the face, and becomes blackness on the face so that everyone sees it.

'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas said: "Indeed, a good deed has a radiance in the face, a light in the heart, expansion in provision, strength in the body, and love in the hearts of creation. And indeed, an evil deed has blackness in the face, darkness in the grave and in the heart, weakness in the body, deficiency in provision, and hatred in the hearts of creation."

Among what sins do is that they weaken the heart and the body. As for their weakening of the heart, this is an obvious matter; indeed, they never stop weakening it until they completely remove its life.

As for their weakening of the body, the believer's strength comes from his heart, and whenever his heart grows strong, his body grows strong. As for the wicked person, although he may be physically strong, he is the weakest of things when need arises, so his strength betrays him at the moment he most needs it. Reflect on the strength of the bodies of Persia and Rome: how it betrayed them when they most needed it, and how the people of faith overcame them by the strength of their bodies and hearts.

Among its consequences is the deprivation of obedience. If sin had no punishment other than that it prevents one from an act of obedience that would have been in its place, and cuts off the path to another act of obedience, then a third path is cut off by sin, then a fourth, and so on, so that many acts of obedience are cut off by sin, each one of which is better for him than this world and all that is in it. This is like a man who ate a meal that caused him a long illness, which prevented him from many better meals. And Allah is the One sought for help.

Among its consequences is that sins shorten the lifespan and surely erase its blessing. Just as righteousness increases the lifespan, debauchery shortens it.

People have differed on this point.

One group said: The decrease in the lifespan of the disobedient person is the loss and erasure of the blessing of his life, and this is true, and it is part of the effect of sins.

Another group said: Rather, it actually decreases it, just as it decreases provision. Allah, glory be to Him, has made many causes for blessing in provision that increase and enlarge it, and causes for blessing in lifespan that increase and enlarge it.

They said: An increase in lifespan is not prevented by causes, just as it is decreased by causes. Provisions and terms, happiness and misery, health and sickness, wealth and poverty, though they are by the decree of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, He decrees what He wills through causes that He has made necessary for their effects and productive of them.

Another group said: The effect of sins on erasing the lifespan is only that the true reality of life is the life of the heart. For this reason Allah, glory be to Him, made the disbeliever dead and not living, as He said, Most High: ﴿They are dead, not alive﴾ [al-Nahl: 21].

So life in reality is the life of the heart, and a person's lifespan is the duration of his living. His lifespan is nothing but the times of his life with Allah, and those are the hours of his lifespan. Righteousness, piety, and obedience increase these times, which are the true reality of his lifespan, and he has no lifespan besides them.

In sum, when the servant turns away from Allah and occupies himself with sins, the true days of his life are lost to him, and he finds the consequence of losing them on the day he says: ﴿Oh, would that I had sent forth for my life﴾ [al-Fajr: 24].

Either he has, along with this, an aspiration toward his worldly and otherworldly interests or he does not. If he has no aspiration toward that, then his whole life is lost to him, and his life has gone in vain. If he has an aspiration toward that, the path grows long for him because of obstacles, and the causes of goodness become difficult for him according to the degree of his occupation with their opposites. That is a real decrease from his lifespan.

The secret of the matter is that a person's lifespan is the duration of his life, and he has no life except by turning toward his Lord, delighting in His love and remembrance, and preferring His pleasure.

**(Section)**

And the words of Allah, Most High: ﴿And We will raise him on the Day of Resurrection blind. He will say, "My Lord, why have You raised me blind, and I had been seeing?"﴾

It has been disputed: is this blindness of insight (basirah) or blindness of sight (basar)?

Those who said it is blindness of insight were moved to that by His saying: ﴿Hear them and see them, the Day they come to Us﴾, and His saying: ﴿You were certainly in heedlessness of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp﴾,

and His saying: ﴿The Day they see the angels, there will be no good news that Day for the criminals﴾, and His saying: ﴿You will surely see Hellfire; then you will surely see it with the certainty of sight﴾.

And similar verses that affirm sight for them in the Hereafter, such as His saying: ﴿And you see them presented before it, humbled by humiliation, looking with a furtive glance﴾, and His saying: ﴿The Day they are pushed toward the Fire of Hell, violently. This is the Fire which you used to deny. Is this magic, or do you not see?﴾,

and His saying: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will think that they are going to fall into it﴾.

Those who preferred that it is blindness of sight said: The context indicates nothing but that.

Because of His saying: ﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You raised me blind, and I had been seeing?"﴾ And he was never seeing in his disbelief at all. Rather, it had become clear to him then that he had been in blindness to the truth in the world. How then would he say, "And I had been seeing"? And how would he be answered with His saying: ﴿Thus Our signs came to you and you forgot them, and thus today you are forgotten﴾?

Rather, this answer contains an indication that it is blindness of sight, and that he was recompensed in kind for his deeds. For when he turned away from the remembrance that Allah sent His Messenger with, and his insight became blind to it, Allah blinded his sight on the Day of Resurrection and left him in punishment, just as he had left remembrance in the world. So He repaid him for the blindness of his insight with blindness of sight in the Hereafter, and for his leaving His remembrance, He left him in punishment.

And Allah, Most High, said: ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one guided, and whomever He leaves astray, you will not find for them protectors other than Him. And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute, and deaf﴾.

It has also been said regarding this verse: they are blind, mute, and deaf to guidance, just as it was said regarding His saying, "And We will raise him on the Day of Resurrection blind," they said: because they will speak that day and hear and see.

As for those who maintained that it is blindness, muteness, and deafness contrary to sight, hearing, and speech, some of them said: it is a restricted, not an absolute, blindness, deafness, and muteness. Thus they are blind to seeing and hearing what would please them. For this reason it has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "They see nothing that would please them."

Others said: This gathering is when the angels take their souls, and they leave the world in that state. Then when they rise from their graves to the place of standing, they rise in that state. Then afterward they will hear and see. This is reported from al-Hasan.

Others said: This only happens when they enter the Fire and settle in it, and their hearing, sight, and speech are taken away, when the Lord, blessed and exalted, says to them: ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾. Then hope is cut off, and their minds become mute, so they all become blind, mute, and deaf, neither seeing, hearing, nor speaking, and nothing is heard from them except the groaning and sighing. This is transmitted from Muqatil.

As for those who said that the intended meaning is blindness to the proof, their intention is only that they have no proof, and they did not mean that they have a proof which they are blind to. Rather, they are blind to guidance, as they were in the world. For the servant dies upon what he lived upon, and is raised upon what he died upon.

By this it becomes clear that the correct position is the other view, that it is blindness of sight. For the disbeliever will know the truth on the Day of Resurrection by direct witnessing, and will acknowledge what he used to deny in the world. So he is not blind to the truth on that day.

The decisive word: gathering (hashr) is joining and assembling, and it is sometimes intended as gathering to the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection.

Like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "You will be gathered to Allah barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised."

Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the wild beasts are gathered﴾, and His saying: ﴿And We shall gather them, and leave not one of them behind﴾.

It means gathering, assembling, and bringing together to the abode of their final destination. So the gathering of the righteous (al-muttaqun) is their gathering and assembling into Paradise, and the gathering of the disbelievers is their gathering and assembling into the Fire. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Day We shall gather the righteous to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Gather those who did wrong, and their spouses, and what they used to worship besides Allah, and lead them to the path of Hellfire﴾.

This gathering is after their gathering to the place of standing (al-mawqif), and it is their gathering and assembling into the Fire. For it has been reported about them that they said: ﴿O woe to us! This is the Day of Recompense.﴾ ﴿This is the Day of Judgment which you used to deny.﴾ Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their spouses﴾, and this is the second gathering.

Accordingly, between the first gathering, from the graves to the place of standing, and the second gathering, from the place of standing to the Fire, they are in different states. At the first gathering they hear, see, dispute, and speak; at the second gathering they are gathered upon their faces, blind, dumb, and deaf. So every station has a condition that befits it and that the justice and wisdom of the Lord, exalted is He, require. The Qur'an confirms one part of it with another: ﴿And had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy.﴾

(Section: On the difference between patience (sabr), self-restraint (tasabbur), steadfast endurance (istibar) and mutual perseverance (musabarah))

The difference between these terms depends on the servant's state within himself and his state with others. If he restrains himself and holds it back from answering the call of what is not good, and this is an innate disposition and a trait that is his own, it is called sabr (patience). If it is done with effort, training, and swallowing its bitterness, it is called tasabbur (forcing oneself to be patient), as this morphological pattern indicates linguistically, for it is coined to denote effort, like tahallum (feigning forbearance), tashja'a (feigning courage), takarrum (feigning generosity), and tahammul (bearing), and the like. When the servant forces it upon himself and seeks it, it becomes a disposition for him, as in the hadith from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "Whoever seeks to be patient, Allah will make him patient." Likewise, the servant forces himself to be chaste until chastity becomes his disposition, and so with all the other traits. This is a matter on which people have differed: can one of these traits be acquired, or does the cultivation of a trait never become a trait in itself? As the poet said:

Desired from the heart is forgetting you, *** but natures refuse the one who transfers them.

And another said:

O you who adorn yourself with what is not your nature, *** indeed, cultivated manners come short of innate character.

So the ugliness of imitation is the nature of the one who is naturally made.

They said: Allah, glory be to Him, has already finished with creation, character, provision, and term of life. Another group said: rather, character can be acquired, just as intellect, forbearance, generosity, liberality, courage, and existence are acquired, and existence bears witness to this. They said: practice yields habits. The meaning of this is that whoever practises something, becomes accustomed to it, and trains himself in it, it becomes his possession, disposition, and nature. They said: habits transform natures, so the servant continues to force himself to be patient until patience becomes his disposition, just as he continues to force himself to forbearance, dignity, tranquility, and steadfastness until they become his characters, in the rank of natures. They said: Allah, glory be to Him, has placed in man the capacity for receiving and learning, so transforming natures away from their requirements is not impossible. Yet this transformation may be weak, so the servant returns to his nature by the slightest motive; it may be strong but without having transformed the nature, so he may return to his nature when the motive becomes stronger and more intense; and the transformation may become so firmly established that its possessor develops a second nature, and such a person can hardly return to the nature he has moved away from.

As for istibar, it is more emphatic than tasabbur, for it is an iftti'al (reflexive form) of sabr, in the rank of acquisition, so tasabbur is the beginning of istibar, just as takassub is the prelude to iktisab. Tasabbur continues to recur until it becomes istibar.

As for musabarah, it is confronting the opponent on the field of patience, for it is a mufa'alah that requires it to occur between two parties, like mushatamah (mutual reviling) and mudaraba (mutual striking). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, be patient, outlast others in patience, stand guard, and fear Allah that you may succeed.﴾

He commanded them to patience, which is the state of the patient person within himself; musabarah, which is his state in patience against his opponent; and murabatah, which is steadfastness, constancy, and staying firm in patience and musabarah. A servant may be patient without outlasting others; or he may outlast others without standing guard; or he may be patient, outlast others, and stand guard without being devoted to taqwa. So Allah, glory be to Him, informed that the essence of all this is taqwa, and that success depends upon it, saying: ﴿and fear Allah that you may succeed.﴾

Just as murabatah is staying at the frontier from which the enemy's attack is feared outwardly, it is also staying at the frontier of the heart, lest desire and Satan enter through it and remove him from his kingdom.
